Name: belief_coherence_geometry
Title: Do LLMs Hold Coherent Beliefs? Probing and Repairing the Internal Geometry of Logically Linked Beliefs
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's belief about a specific item is not stored in isolation but participates in an internal belief network; we hypothesize that (a) logically entailed beliefs (P and its consequences) share a partially aligned representational subspace, (b) belief-vs-fact failures and self-contradictions arise when the model encodes a belief in P without propagating it to logically-linked propositions (a 'coherence gap' measurable as low subspace alignment), and (c) this coherence gap is causally repairable by a lightweight propagation intervention that aligns linked-belief representations, reducing self-contradiction without harming factual QA.
Related Work: Suzgun et al. ('Belief in the Machine'/KaBLE) and the referenced 'Language models cannot reliably distinguish belief from knowledge and fact' establish behavioral belief-knowledge-fact conflation but treat each proposition's belief as an isolated one-shot judgment, never asking whether beliefs about logically-linked propositions are mutually coherent. Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark; Savcisens & Eliassi-Rad 'Trilemma of Truth'; Schouten et al.) recovers per-statement veracity axes but does not model relationships between beliefs. Behavioral consistency benchmarks (e.g., BeliefBank, negation/implication consistency, LM logical-consistency tests) measure whether stated answers are consistent but do not probe or causally manipulate an *internal* representation of belief coherence, nor localize where in the network coherence breaks. Knowledge-editing work (MEMIT/MQuAKE) studies ripple effects of edits but not the native geometric coherence of pre-existing beliefs. My prior proposals covered agent-attribution, update inertia, item-truth binding, temporal indexing, source provenance, and graded epistemic strength; none address the *relational coherence* of a belief with its logical neighbors. We recast belief-vs-fact failures as a belief-propagation/coherence problem in representation space, a genuinely new lens.
Abstract: Coherent agents propagate a belief to its logical consequences: if you believe a whale is a mammal, you should believe it is not a fish. Existing work shows LLMs conflate belief, knowledge, and fact, but treats an LLM's belief about an item as an isolated truth-value, ignoring whether logically-linked beliefs cohere. We ask whether LLMs internally maintain a coherent belief network and whether self-contradictions and belief-vs-fact errors stem from a failure to propagate a belief to its logical neighbors. Using controlled sets of logically-linked propositions (entailments, negations, transitive chains, mutual exclusions) built around specific items, we probe residual-stream activations across several open-weight models. We train per-proposition belief probes and measure the alignment of belief-representation subspaces across logically-linked propositions, defining a 'coherence gap' as low alignment where high alignment is logically required. We find that (1) logically entailed beliefs share partially aligned subspaces, (2) large coherence gaps predict behavioral self-contradiction and belief-vs-fact errors better than per-statement truth-confidence, and (3) a lightweight propagation intervention that steers a target belief's representation toward the subspace of its logical antecedent reduces self-contradiction and repairs downstream answers without harming unrelated factual QA. We introduce coherence-gap and internal-contradiction-rate metrics and localize where coherence breaks across layers. This reframes belief-vs-fact confusion as an internal belief-propagation problem and offers a cheap, interpretable fix. All experiments run on <=9B open-weight models feasible for an academic lab.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Build clusters of logically-linked propositions about specific items across four relation types: (i) ENTAILMENT (P => Q, e.g., 'X is a whale' => 'X is a mammal'), (ii) NEGATION (P vs not-P), (iii) TRANSITIVE CHAINS (A>B, B>C => A>C), (iv) MUTUAL EXCLUSION (X cannot be both A and B). Use factual clusters (from taxonomies/WordNet, spatial relations) and neutral/fictional clusters to separate parametric priors from in-context logic. ~2-3k proposition clusters with entity/order/paraphrase randomization and single-proposition controls. 2) Behavioral coherence analysis: Query the model's belief on each proposition in a cluster independently; define internal-contradiction-rate = fraction of clusters where stated beliefs violate the logical relation (e.g., believes P but denies its entailment Q). Measure how contradiction-rate scales with chain length, relation type, and factual-vs-fictional content; compare first- vs third-person and belief-vs-fact phrasings. Models: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, plus a base-vs-chat pair. 3) Internal geometry: Extract residual-stream activations at each proposition's query position; train linear/logistic belief probes per proposition. For each logically-linked pair, compute belief-subspace alignment (cosine between probe-decoded belief directions / principal angles between per-relation activation subspaces). Define the coherence-gap as the alignment deficit relative to what the logical relation requires (high alignment for entailment/transitivity, anti-alignment for negation/exclusion). Report per-layer coherence-gap to localize where coherence breaks. 4) Error-geometry link: Test whether coherence-gap predicts behavioral contradiction (AUC) beyond a per-statement truth-confidence baseline. 5) Causal propagation intervention: (a) Activation patching — patch the belief subspace of a logical antecedent into the consequent's query position and test whether the consequent's answer becomes coherent (flip-rate) while unrelated propositions stay fixed (specificity). (b) Steering — add a 'propagation' direction (difference-of-means from coherent vs incoherent linked pairs) and measure controllability and specificity. 6) Lightweight fix: A small LoRA fine-tune (or steering-only) with an auxiliary loss that increases belief-subspace alignment for entailed pairs and anti-alignment for negations/exclusions; evaluate internal-contradiction-rate reduction, coherence-gap reduction, and retained factual QA (MMLU/TriviaQA subset) and logical-consistency benchmarks (BeliefBank-style). Metrics: internal-contradiction-rate, coherence-gap, per-layer break localization, probe accuracy, prediction AUC, patch/steer flip-rate and specificity, retained factual/consistency accuracy.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Stated belief may not equal internal belief; mitigated by pairing behavioral contradiction with probe-decoded belief and reporting divergences. 2) Belief-subspace alignment may reflect topical/lexical similarity rather than genuine logical propagation; mitigated by matched controls with topically-similar but logically-unlinked pairs and by fictional clusters. 3) Linear probes may miss nonlinear belief encoding; we also try MLP probes and report negatives as informative. 4) The expected alignment sign per relation type (positive for entailment, negative for negation) may be more nuanced; we validate on clean single-proposition and few-relation controls before scaling. 5) Propagation steering may have off-target effects; specificity/retention metrics quantify this. 6) Effects may vary across model families, relation types, and scale; we report per-condition results rather than universal claims.
